0c47394cda7f92f1: Gallery Esther Schipper presents the exhibition 'Repose' by artist David Claerbout, which opens on Thursday, September 10, 2026. Under the title 'Repose,' the exhibition showcases four works that are being shown in Berlin for the first time: 'The woodcarver and the forest' (2025), 'Birdcage' (2023), 'Backwards Growing Tree' (2023), and 'Eagle Eye' (2026). In addition to the videos, a series of works on paper will also be displayed. All the films presented explore our relationship with nature and the way we learn to see the world around us. In 'The woodcarver and the forest,' we observe a woodcarver cutting wooden blocks to create one spoon after another; the narrative works almost meditatively until we realize that each gesture has a price: outside his window, the forest slowly turns into the objects he is making. The lush gardens of a noble estate, on display in 'Birdcage,' become the stage for a violent breakout, transforming the scene (and the audience) from apparent calm into a state of tension and fear. David Claerbout, Repose, Esther Schipper, 2026. Photo © Andrea Rossetti. David Claerbout, Bonn, 2026, Courtesy of the artist and Esther Schipper In 'Eagle Eye,' a bald eagle is awake but motionless on an operating table, which turns our usual association of the eagle as a symbol of strength and freedom on its head. Through found footage, CGI, and generative AI, Claerbout brings the computer-generated and the organic together, blurring the line between a living being being observed and a model that has learned to observe. 424771748e768dd4: Gallery Friese presents from Friday, September 11, 2026 (Opening: September 10.). The exhibition URFORM by artist Claire de Santa Coloma. Gallery Friese presents the third solo exhibition of Claire de Santa Coloma at Gallery Friese as part of Berlin Art Week 2026. In the exhibition 'Urform', the Argentine sculptor shows an installation of her wooden sculptures that span several rooms. Claire de Santa Coloma (*1983 in Buenos Aires) works around materiality, space, and perception. The starting point is the found piece of wood, which the artist works on as little as possible by hand. Each piece tells something about its origin and the relationship between humans and their environment. The sculptures of Santa Colomas remind of polished stones from the water, of organs or eggs - archaic 'primordial forms', as familiar as if they had always existed. Forms that seem to precede the human and yet are needed for him to appear. At the same time, they stand in the tradition of Classical Modernism, particularly Brâncuși's iconic abstract form language, to which Claire de Santa Coloma also refers in her installation-oriented settings. 'Primordial Form' gathers the sculptures as space-based, touchable installations. The specially designed, table-like bases for the exhibition lead through the gallery spaces. Walking, touching, thinking - the works call for the entire body, not just the eyes. The forms continuously transform, are related to each other and yet never identical. A process without a goal, carried by the necessity of making itself, the ever-renewed attempt to approach one form. […]
59740e806fa3c5e5: In February 2016, Yadegar Asisi made her first trip to Antarctica - a region known for its extreme living conditions as well as its overwhelming beauty and monumental silence. Exactly ten years later, on 24 January, his new panorama exhibition ANTARCTICA opened at the Panometer Leipzig. The 32-metre-high circular image takes visitors to one of the most hostile and fascinating regions on earth - where water and ice meet in the Antarctic coastal landscape. Huge ice formations and glaciers tower above the water's surface in the 360°panorama, while a fragile and astonishingly diverse ecosystem with numerous marine animals reveals itself underneath. The visual experience is intensified in the panoramic image with a 15-minute day and night simulation. Light changes, auroras, matching background noises and music bring the scenery to life and give you the feeling of immersing yourself up close in this overwhelming landscape. The giant picture is complemented by an accompanying exhibition with photographs, exhibits and drawings. They illuminate climate, geology and wildlife as well as Yadegar Asisi's personal, artistic access to this unique continent.

5b392495ca772cbf: Taubert Contemporary will present the exhibition "DIFFERENTLEVELSOFBEING" by artist Markus Linnenbrink from Thursday, September 10, 2026. These "Photo Drips" are based on photographs taken by Linnenbrink in 2023 at the Museum für Naturkunde in Berlin. They depict stuffed animals and museum exhibits, whose silent presence oscillates between scientific documentation and aesthetic presentation. Among them are a large cat, a zebra, a bird, and shelves full of reagent flasks - motifs that illustrate the diversity of natural history collections and simultaneously reveal different forms of conservation, organization, and classification. The photographs are applied to the support surfaces and then coated with a transparent layer of epoxy resin; afterward, Linnenbrink applies his characteristic epoxy stripes. In this process, painting and photography merge into a single image plane where documentation, materiality, and color flow into each other. The flowing color layers do not conceal the motif but rather change its perception. They create a tension between visibility and concealment, between stillness and movement. The photographic image remains present but is transformed into a new spatial and temporal context by the color. The animals no longer appear exclusively as natural history exhibits but as carriers of images, whose meaning constantly changes through the process of painterly overlay. Markus Linnenbrink, DIFFERENTLEVELSOFBEING, installation view: Martin Müller, Berlin. Courtesy of the Gallery. […]
605a42b9be887b84: The collection of the Leipziger Hof occupies a special place among the private collections of German art of the 20th century, as it contains numerous main works of painting of the "Leipziger Schule". In almost complete unity, the collection presents in particular the painting of the short, eruptive phase of young German history, the Reunification period - both art-historically and as a contemporary historical document. The founder of the hotel and retired Munich physics professor Dr. Klaus Eberhard compiled the more than 350 works in the years from 1990 to the present in close cooperation with the city's museums and with Leipzig art historians. Despite being hung in a hotel, the intimate, private character of the collection has been preserved. Probably also because Eberhard never acquired "en bloc" and only aesthetic aspects and the quality of the exhibits - often reassured by the judgment of friendly art historians - were and are the main features of the collection. Works by more than 70 Leipzig artists are shown - the spectrum ranges from the "fathers" of the Leipzig School such as Heisig, Mattheuer, Mayer-Foreyt and Tübke to Gille, Rink, Ebersbach, Minkewitz and Müller-Simon to the young, globally celebrated artists of the "New Leipzig School" such as Weischer, Triegel, Loy and others. The collection is constantly being supplemented.

8b30c62aacf79d7d: The Leipzig Codex is one of the most famous Hebrew manuscripts that have survived from the Middle Ages. Now, for the first time in 17 years, the opportunity to see the Leipzig Codex has returned. For the opening, there will be a discussion evening on the superlative Jewish cultural heritage, the tangled paths of ownership history, and the responsibility that arises from it today. With Prof. Jörg Deventer, Deputy Director at the Leibniz Institute for Jewish History and Culture - Simon Dubnow, and Dr. Christoph Mackert, Director of the Manuscripts Center of the University Library Leipzig. On the closing day, October 25, Katrin Kogman-Appel, Humboldt Professor of Jewish Studies at the University of Münster and one of the most internationally renowned experts on Hebrew manuscripts, will tell about her research on the Leipziger Machsor and explain what makes this manuscript unique. As part of 'Tacheles. Year of Jewish Culture in Saxony 2026'.

b2924520d6c65453: Heidi Specker approaches this exhibition of the person and work of Aenne Biermann (1898-1933), artistically and personally relating to her. Aenne Biermann was a special figure in the city society of Gera - in the 1920s a cosmopolitan place and cultural center of modernity. In just a few years, an autodidact had become an important representative of avant-garde photography. She wore her hair short, a 'man's cut', and had her working room designed by one of the most renowned architects of her time. Her photographs depict 'The New Vision', that is, intensive observation of the immediate environment as well as unusual perspectives on people and things. Aenne Biermann's work was abruptly interrupted by her early death due to illness. A large part of her photographic legacy was stolen by the Nazis or is considered lost. In the course of her artistic research, Heidi Specker traveled to Gera, Trieste, and Vienna and made contact with the grandchildren of Aenne Biermann. In juxtapositions, she perceives themes and compositions of the photographer, adapts them, and translates them into the present. Two video works tell of important stages of her trail hunt.

eeaaec4dfc5f2e8a: Bright flowers, finely drawn landscapes, portraits with a deep view - Margarethe Freudenberg (1876 - 1939) created well over a hundred watercolours, drawings and oil paintings in just seven years. Born in Berlin as a contemporary of Paula Modersohn-Becker, she received drawing lessons in her hometown from the painters Franz Skarbina and Ludwig Dettmann. In 1899 she became engaged, married and had six children in the following years. She gave up painting. Only after her death did her children find the drawings and watercolors hidden in an attic. Today, many works have been preserved or rediscovered and have been brought to light in two exhibitions. For the first time, the images of great gift and creative power could be seen in public. For the 150th Birthday of Margarethe Freudenberg, this anniversary exhibition presents a selection of the versatile work and pays tribute to an unknown artist. The exhibition will be inaugurated on its birthday, July 31, in the presence of the descendants.
efa5a2e68fe1add0: The exhibition illuminates artists' positions from the GDR and invites viewers to read art from the GDR anew. Through the fluctuating biographies of nine artists and their works – including paintings, sculptures, ceramics, and photographs – it shows how differently the artists navigated the political and social conditions of their time. To what extent did sexual orientation influence their artistic practice and professional development? Homosexuality remained in the GDR, despite gradual decriminalization, strongly stigmatized socially and politically. After the fall of the Berlin Wall, the situation for queer artists did not significantly improve – rather, many artists from the GDR were at risk of being forgotten. Today, there is growing general interest in the art and culture of the GDR as well as in queer life realities. Although the term 'queer' in its current meaning did not exist in the GDR, it is consciously used in the exhibition: as a collective term for people who, as lesbians, gays, and bisexuals, desired and loved the same sex, as well as for those who lived as transgender and non-binary individuals beyond conventional gender conceptions.

fcbf108428db73c7: Galerie Société presents the exhibition 'Sugarshack' by artist Salim Green from Friday, September 1, 2026 (Opening: September 10.). Salim Green describes his interdisciplinary practice as a process in which 'things are defined by their contours.' In his work, he frequently draws on speculative models such as the 'Dark Forest Theory' and related concepts to process lived experiences. With their persistent focus on the unrecognizability and interiority, Green's works resist the magnetism of fixed meanings or clearly defined identifications and rely on strategies of concealment, opacity, and illegibility, which stem from the experience of Black people. The title 'Sugarshack' refers to an expression used by the artist's father to describe abandoned or decaying buildings in his hometown of Waterloo, Iowa. As a significant production and industrial center in the Midwest, Waterloo became a destination for African Americans during the 'Great Migration,' who left the racially segregated South; many were recruited by the railroad to break strikes. For the newcomers, freight cars were provided as temporary housing alongside the tracks in the eastern part of the city before they built their homes in the same area - the only part of the city that was open to them at the time due to restrictive housing regulations in Waterloo - many of which have since left.
